The story uses the exact principle described in the background information: taking a character who initially appears to be a one-dimensional stereotype and transforming them into a complex, believable human being. 

At the beginning of the story, Q is presented as an archetype—the effortless, aristocratic "golden boy" who glides through life without friction. However, during the poolside scene ten years later, the author peels back this layer to reveal Q's weaknesses, anxieties, and cowardice, transforming him into a round, complex character (a pathetic middle manager who avoids conflict by firing an employee at a beach club without even reading the briefing packet). 

The narrator also evolves, moving from insecure, "fascinated passivity" to a grounded sense of relief when he realizes Q is subject to the same "gravity" as everyone else. 

Even the minor characters are developed to an appropriate level of complexity for their roles. Meredith, though only present for one scene, is given distinct clothing, a midwestern voice, a fiancé, a strong work ethic, and a sharp, realistic reaction to Q's manipulation. Rather than feeling like a mere plot device, she feels like a real person with "bones and weight." Finally, peripheral characters like Arthur and Clara are given just enough specific detail (Arthur being a newly divorced tax attorney who loves fluke crudo) to make the world feel lived-in without distracting from the central narrative.
